title: Connect Codex to Self-Managed Airbyte Core with the Airbyte MCP
summary: Run the Airbyte MCP server locally so Codex can list connections, read failed job logs, and build pipelines on Airbyte Core, without putting your secrets in its config.
body_markdown:
You run Airbyte Core with` abctl` on a VM or your laptop and when a sync fails, you probably open the UI, select the connection, scroll through the job log, and copy the error into a search engine to figure out why. With the Airbyte MCP, Codex can sift through those logs and search for answers independently. It can:


- List your connections
- Pull the failed job's log
- Explain the error


All that before you need to open a browser tab.


The hosted Airbyte MCP at` https://mcp.airbyte.com/mcp` only talks to Airbyte Cloud; if you’re on Core, you’ll need to manually give Codex your client ID and secret. Our setup docs put those values directly in your MCP client’s config file. That works, but it puts a long-lived secret in a file you may copy between machines, share with teammates, or check into a dotfiles repo.


This tutorial offers an alternative. In it, I’ll show you how to run the Airbyte MCP server on your own machine and point it at your Core deployment's API. Codex starts the server for you over stdio. You'll keep your Airbyte credentials in an env file outside your project. You’ll also configure approval prompts and secret references to allow Codex to deploy a source without seeing your password.


## Prerequisites


While you don't need prior experience with MCP or Codex configuration, you will need the following:


- A running Airbyte Core deployment.
- Codex CLI installed and signed in.
- A UNIX terminal environment. If you’re on a Windows machine, you can run Codex and the server inside WSL. That way, you can use the same commands without the translation into PowerShell syntax.
- ` uv` , which downloads and runs the Airbyte MCP server. If you use Homebrew,` brew install uv` works.
- Internet access from the machine running Codex. The server installs from PyPI and looks up connectors in Airbyte's registry.


## Step 1: Collect your workspace ID and API credentials


The local server signs in to Airbyte with an application's client ID and secret. Core has no browser sign-in for the MCP. So do the following instead:


1. Open Airbyte in your browser. On a new deployment, finish the setup page and enter your email address. The Airbyte MCP can't find your default workspace until your user has one.
2. Copy the alphanumeric string after` /workspaces/` in the URL of any workspace page. You’ll use this as the` WORKSPACE_ID` in the` .env` file.
3. Get a client ID and client secret:


- If you deployed with` abctl` , run` abctl local credentials` and copy the` Client-Id` and` Client-Secret` values.
- Otherwise, create an application and copy its client ID and secret.


4. Note your API URL. It's your Airbyte URL followed by` /api/public/v1` . The` abctl` default is` http://localhost:8000/api/public/v1` .


You now have the four values the server needs. Keep them out of your terminal history and chat for the next step.


## Step 2: Store the credentials in an env file outside your project


The server reads an env file named by` AIRBYTE_MCP_ENV_FILE` , so the secret never has to appear in Codex's` config.toml` . Put the file in its own directory away from any repository Codex works in. The steps below create the file and folder inside your user directory.


Create a private directory and an empty file:


BASH


```text
mkdir   -p ~/.airbyte-mcp
chmod   700 ~/.airbyte-mcp
touch   ~/.airbyte-mcp/core.env
chmod   600 ~/.airbyte-mcp/core.env
```


Open` ~/.airbyte-mcp/core.env` in your editor and add your values:


~/.airbyte-mcp/core.env


INI


```text
AIRBYTE_CLOUD_API_URL  =http://localhost: 8000  /api/public/v1
AIRBYTE_CLOUD_CLIENT_ID  =<CLIENT_ID>
AIRBYTE_CLOUD_CLIENT_SECRET  =<CLIENT_SECRET>
AIRBYTE_CLOUD_WORKSPACE_ID  =<WORKSPACE_ID>
```


The variables say` CLOUD` because the server shares its code with the hosted version. Point` AIRBYTE_CLOUD_API_URL` at your own deployment to switch it to Core. Always set` AIRBYTE_CLOUD_WORKSPACE_ID` ; without it, tools that need a workspace can fail with errors.


Your credentials now live in one file that only your user can read.


## Step 3: Register the server with Codex


Codex can add a stdio server from the command line. The` --` separates Codex's flags from the command that starts the server.


TYPESCRIPT


```text
codex mcp add airbyte \
--env  AIRBYTE_MCP_ENV_FILE  = /Users/  <you> /.airbyte-mcp/  core. env
-- uvx --python= 3.12   -- from  =airbyte @latest   airbyte-mcp
```


` uvx --from=airbyte@latest airbyte-mcp` downloads the airbyte package into a cached environment and starts its MCP server. To pin a version for your team, replace` @latest` with an exact version such as` airbyte==0.71.2` .


You may have noticed that I pinned the Python version to 3.12. The package doesn’t yet support Python 3.13+ just yet.


Use an absolute path for` AIRBYTE_MCP_ENV_FILE` . The server doesn't expand` ~` or` $HOME` because Codex launches it outside a shell.


That command writes an entry to` ~/.codex/config.toml` . Open the file and add two timeouts so the entry looks like this:


~/.codex/config.toml


INI


```text
[mcp_servers.airbyte]
command   =  "uvx"
args   = [ "--from=airbyte@latest"  ,  "airbyte-mcp"  ]
startup_timeout_sec   =  60
tool_timeout_sec   =  300
default_tools_approval_mode   =  "writes"


[mcp_servers.airbyte.env]
AIRBYTE_MCP_ENV_FILE   =  "/Users/<you>/.airbyte-mcp/core.env"
AIRBYTE_MCP_TRUSTED_EXECUTION   =  "1"
```


Here's what each setting does:


- ` startup_timeout_sec = 60` gives the server time to start. Codex waits 10 seconds by default. In our testing, the first launch took about 30 seconds while uv installed the package, and later launches with` @latest` still took about 15 seconds while uv checked for updates. With the default, Codex gives up before the server is ready.
- ` tool_timeout_sec = 300` covers slow calls like reading a long job log. The default is 30 seconds.
- ` default_tools_approval_mode = "writes"` makes Codex prompt you before any write tool, so you approve each deploy, config change, and sync.
- ` AIRBYTE_MCP_TRUSTED_EXECUTION = "1"` lets the server treat your env file as a secret store. Codex can see the variable names through` list_dotenv_secrets` , which returns names only, and can pass` secret_reference::<password>` in a connector config. The server swaps in the real value when it calls your Airbyte API.


If you want to lock the agent down to read only functionality, replace this field with` AIRBYTE_CLOUD_MCP_READONLY_MODE = "1"` and delete` AIRBYTE_MCP_TRUSTED_EXECUTION = "1"` .


To make the first launch faster, warm the uv cache before you start Codex:


TYPESCRIPT


```text
uvx --python= 3.13   -- from  =airbyte @latest   airbyte-mcp <  /dev/  null
```


The server starts, sees no input, and exits. The package stays cached.


Codex now knows how to start the Airbyte MCP and where to find its credentials.


## Step 4: Confirm the connection


Check that Codex sees the entry with the following command:


CODE


```text
codex mcp list
```


You should see` airbyte` as enabled. Don’t worry about the` Unsupported` value in the Auth column. That’s just for remote servers using a browser to sign in. Codex will instead be using the credentials in the env file to sign in.


Start Codex with` codex` , then type` /mcp` to see the active servers.` airbyte` should be listed with its tools.


Send a first prompt:


Prompt


CSS


```text
Which Airbyte workspace am  I   connected  to  ? List the sources, destinations,
and connections in it, grouped by type.
```


Codex calls` get_default_cloud_context` and the` list_deployed_cloud_*` tools and returns your inventory.


The MCP works a little differently on Core than it does on cloud. You can find the full list of differences here. The major differences to expect are:


- **Links include /api/public/v1.** Links to Airbyte that the server returns point at the API path, so they error in your browser. Delete` /api/public/v1` from the link to open the page.
- **Billing tools fail.**` get_cloud_organization_billing_status` only works in Airbyte Cloud.
- **No context layer.** Direct reads from sources and destinations and connector skills are Cloud-only.


If` /mcp` doesn't show the server, run` codex mcp get airbyte` to check the entry, and run` which uvx` in your terminal. If Codex can't find` uvx` on its PATH, set` command` to the full path that` which` prints.


Codex is now connected to your Core deployment and can read and write to your Airbyte Core deployment.


## Step 5: Build a connection using Airbyte MCP


On top of troubleshooting pipelines, you can also now use Codex to create custom connectors, configure sources and destinations, and build pipelines. If you want to complete the connector configuration directly from Codex, add the source’s secret to your` core.env` file. For example, add a Postgres password with the following variable:


INI


```text
POSTGRES_PASSWORD  =<password>
```


Now ask Codex to build something:


Prompt


SQL


```text
List the secret names available  to   you.  Then   deploy a Postgres source named
"orders-db"  with   host db.internal, port  5432  , database orders, username
airbyte_reader,  and   the password  from   secret_reference::POSTGRES_PASSWORD.
Never print  or   ask  for   the password value. Run a  check    on   the source,  then
create   a connection  to   my existing warehouse destination  with   the orders  and
customers streams selected,  and    start    one   sync.
```


Codex calls` list_dotenv_secrets` ,` deploy_source_to_cloud` ,` check_cloud_source` ,` create_connection_on_cloud` , and` run_cloud_sync` with approval gates at every write action. The password goes from your env file to your Airbyte API without passing through the conversation.


Be aware that the server guards against deletes. Tools that permanently delete sources, destinations, connections, or custom connector definitions only run when the resource's name contains` delete-me` or` deleteme` , which means you’ll need to rename a resource yourself in the UI to let Codex remove it.


If you want, you can remove the requirement that deletions have` deleteme` in their name. Seeing as we included this default, though, we don’t recommend removing it.


## Takeaways


Running the Airbyte MCP locally gives Codex most of the pipeline tools on Core that Cloud users get from the hosted server: inventory, job history, logs, deploys, connections, and syncs. Airbyte Core permissions don’t have the role-based restrictions that they do for Airbyte Cloud, though, so make sure your agent only has the ability to do exactly what it needs to.


To keep access as safe as possible, use the following guidelines:


- **Split monitoring from building.** Register two entries,` airbyte-ro` with read-only mode for daily checks and` airbyte` with write access for pipeline work, and enable the second only when you need it.
- **Share one config with your team.** Pin the airbyte version in` args` , commit a` config.toml` snippet with a placeholder env file path, and have each person keep their own env file.
- **Report what breaks.** If you hit an issue that isn't in the known issues list, open an Airbyte MCP issue, and leave secrets out of it.


For setup on Airbyte Cloud, see Install the Airbyte MCP.
